opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and I think it's one where the analogy to language models is useful, but only up to a point.

The way I think about it is that a pretrained foundation model for structured data, for relational databases, gives you a really strong starting point. You point it at your database, it understands the tables, the primary key/foreign key relationships, the temporal structure, and with in-context learning it can make a pretty good prediction right away, with no training at all. For many use cases that's already a huge win, because what used to take a data science team weeks or months of feature engineering and pipeline building, you can now get in seconds.

But then the question is: what's the value of going further and fine-tuning on your specific data and your specific task? What we see is that fine-tuning still adds meaningful accuracy. The pretrained model has learned general patterns: how recency matters, how frequency matters, how signals propagate across linked entities. Every business, though, has its own idiosyncrasies. Your customers behave a certain way, your product catalog has a particular structure, your churn definition is specific to you. When you fine-tune, the model can specialize to those patterns, and you typically get a nice lift over the zero-shot or in-context version.

So I think of it as a spectrum. On one end, you have the pretrained model used out of the box, which is great for exploration, prototyping, and asking lots of predictive questions quickly. You can basically query your data predictively, the way you'd write a SQL query. On the other end, when you find a task that really matters, say a recommendation system or fraud detection that's running in production and driving real revenue, then it's absolutely worth investing in fine-tuning, because those last few points of accuracy translate directly into business value.

The other interesting thing is that fine-tuning a foundation model is much more efficient than training from scratch. You converge faster, you need less labeled data, and you're more robust, especially in cold-start situations or for tasks where labels are sparse. The pretraining acts as a very strong prior.

And I'd say, just like in language, this is still evolving. We're figuring out the right recipes for post-training these models: how much task-specific data you need, how to adapt to new schemas, how to keep the general capabilities while specializing. But the big picture is clear: pretraining gives you breadth and speed, and fine-tuning gives you depth and that last mile of performance where it matters most.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, and I think the way to frame it is to first ask what a foundation model for structured data even is, because it's really different from language.

With language, the pretraining already gets you most of the way. The model has read the internet, it has an enormous amount of world knowledge, and post-training is mostly about shaping behavior, aligning it, making it follow instructions. With relational data, with enterprise databases, the situation is almost reversed. Every company's database is its own little universe. The schemas are different, the column names are different, the semantics of what a "customer" or a "transaction" means are different. There is no public corpus of relational databases that looks like your company's data. So a pretrained relational foundation model, what it learns is something more like the grammar of structured data: how entities relate across tables through primary and foreign keys, how time works, how to aggregate signals over a neighborhood of linked records. It learns to reason over the structure. But it doesn't know the specifics of your business.

So that's where fine-tuning becomes really valuable. In language you can often get away with prompting. In structured data, I'd argue the specifics matter a lot more, and fine-tuning on even a modest amount of your own labeled data, say your historical churn outcomes or your fraud labels, lets the model adapt from that general understanding of structure to the particular distribution and particular quirks of your data. And what we see is that the gains from that step can be substantial. The pretrained model gives you a very strong zero-shot baseline, which by the way is already a huge deal because traditionally you'd spend months on feature engineering before you had any model at all. But fine-tuning is where you close the gap to, and often exceed, what a team would get from a hand-built pipeline.

The other thing I'd say is that fine-tuning in this setting is a much lighter-weight operation than people are used to from the deep learning world. You're not retraining a huge network from scratch. You're adapting a model that already knows how to read your schema, so the data requirements and compute requirements are small, and the iteration loop is fast. That changes the economics. Instead of one or two predictive models a company can afford to build and maintain, you can have dozens, one per business question, all sitting on top of the same foundation model.

And then the last benefit, which I think is underappreciated, is that post-training is where you inject the task definition itself. In structured data the task is really just a query: predict this column, for these entities, at this point in time. So the fine-tuning signal is essentially the business logic, expressed as data rather than as code. That's a really nice separation, because the heavy lifting of learning representations is done once, and the thing that varies, what you actually want to predict, is cheap to specify and cheap to change.

astra-6.text:
I think the key benefit is adaptation. A foundation model gives you a starting point, but structured data is very specific to the organization and the problem you want to solve. You have particular tables, relationships between entities, and a particular notion of what you want to predict.

Post-training lets you adapt that starting point to the data and the task. For example, predicting whether a customer will buy something is different from predicting whether a transaction is fraudulent, even if some of the underlying data overlaps. Fine-tuning gives the model a way to learn which patterns and relationships matter for that particular prediction.

The exciting possibility is that you don’t have to build a separate model from scratch for every task. You can reuse what the foundation model has learned and then specialize it with the examples you have. Of course, the question is how much that actually helps: Does it improve accuracy, does it require fewer labeled examples, and does it reduce the work needed to deploy a useful model? Those are the benefits I would want to measure.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key benefit is that you can separate learning general patterns from learning what matters for a particular task. With structured data, you have tables, relationships between entities, and often a lot of history. A foundation model can learn from that context, but the downstream question is usually very specific: Which customer will churn? Which transaction should we investigate? What will happen to this entity next?

Fine-tuning gives you a way to adapt those representations to the outcome you care about, using the labeled examples you have. The hope is that you need fewer examples because the model already understands something about the underlying data and its relationships.

But I would distinguish adapting to a task from adapting to a new database. Different databases have different schemas and different meanings attached to their columns and relationships. So an important question is how much of that adaptation the foundation model can handle directly, and where additional training actually improves performance. Ultimately, you want to measure that benefit on the downstream prediction task.
